title: Allow/Deny Policies & Rate/Spend Limits
summary: Beyond sandboxing individual tools, you need a policy layer that governs the whole agent: an allow/deny list of what tools may run, per-user and per-session rate and budget limits on how often and how expensively they run, and a kill switch to stop everything instantly. A policy-enforcing dispatcher sits in front of every tool call, decides allow or deny against these rules, meters usage, and refuses once a limit or the kill switch trips.

subtopics.title: A policy layer sits above the tools
subtopics.explanation: Rather than scattering checks inside each tool, you place a single policy layer between the agent and every tool it can call, so one component decides whether a given call is permitted right now. Centralizing the decision means the rules are consistent, auditable, and changeable without touching tool code. This layer is the chokepoint that makes allow/deny, rate limits, and budgets enforceable as a system rather than as scattered good intentions.

subtopics.title: Allow/deny lists: default-deny wins
subtopics.explanation: The policy names which tools are permitted, and the safe design is default-deny: only tools on an explicit allow list may run, and anything else — including a hallucinated or newly added tool — is refused. A deny list alone always misses something, whereas an allow list fails closed when in doubt. Defaulting to deny is what stops an agent from invoking capabilities you never intended to expose.
subtopics.example:
ALLOW = {"search", "read_file", "summarize"}   # explicitly permitted
DENY  = {"run_shell"}                          # explicitly forbidden

def allowed(action: str) -> bool:
    if action in DENY:
        return False
    return action in ALLOW      # default-deny: unknown -> not allowed

print(allowed("search"))      # True
print(allowed("run_shell"))   # False
print(allowed("delete_all"))  # False -- unknown, so denied

subtopics.title: Rate limits per user and per session
subtopics.explanation: Even allowed tools must not be called without bound, so you meter calls per user and per session against a rate limit — for example N calls per minute — and reject once the count is exceeded. Scoping the counter to the right key (user, session, or tool) prevents one runaway loop or one abusive user from starving everyone else. Rate limiting is the control that keeps a stuck or hostile agent from hammering a downstream API into the ground.
subtopics.example:
import time
from collections import defaultdict

calls = defaultdict(list)   # key -> list of timestamps

def under_rate_limit(key: str, limit: int, window: float = 60.0) -> bool:
    now = time.time()
    calls[key] = [t for t in calls[key] if now - t < window]  # drop old
    if len(calls[key]) >= limit:
        return False           # too many calls in the window
    calls[key].append(now)
    return True

print(under_rate_limit("user:42", limit=3))  # True until the 4th call/min

subtopics.title: Token and dollar budgets
subtopics.explanation: Because model and tool usage costs real money, the policy tracks token and dollar spend per user or session and refuses further calls once the budget is spent. You estimate a call's cost before running it and check it against the remaining budget, so a single agent can never rack up an unbounded bill. Budget enforcement is what turns 'we should watch our costs' into a hard ceiling the agent cannot exceed.

subtopics.title: Kill switches and the enforcing dispatcher
subtopics.explanation: A kill switch is a single flag that, when set, makes the policy deny every call instantly — your emergency stop when something goes wrong in production. The enforcing dispatcher ties it all together: it checks the kill switch, the allow/deny list, the rate limit, and the budget in order, and only if all pass does it run the tool and record the usage. This dispatcher is the concrete artifact that makes every policy above impossible for the agent to route around.

foundations.overview: Sandboxing constrains what a single tool can do; a policy layer governs the agent as a whole. It answers three questions for every tool call: is this tool allowed at all, is the caller within their rate limit, and are they within their token/dollar budget — plus a kill switch that can deny everything at once. The design principle throughout is default-deny and fail-closed: only allowlisted tools run, unknown or newly added tools are refused, and any ambiguity resolves to 'no'. Rate limits scoped per user and per session stop a runaway loop or an abusive caller from hammering downstream systems, and budgets tracked per user/session put a hard ceiling on spend so no single agent run can produce an unbounded bill. All of this is enforced by a policy-enforcing dispatcher that intercepts every call, checks the kill switch, allow/deny list, rate limit, and budget in order, and only then invokes the tool and meters the usage. The dispatcher is the one chokepoint the agent cannot bypass, which is what turns these policies from aspirations into hard controls.
foundations.formalDefinition: A policy layer is a mediation component that authorizes each agent tool call against a set of rules — an allow/deny list of permitted tools, per-scope rate limits (calls per time window), and per-scope token/dollar budgets — and a global kill switch. A policy-enforcing dispatcher applies these checks in order for every call, denying (raising) on any failure and otherwise executing the tool and recording its usage against the counters.
foundations.whyItMatters: An autonomous agent can loop, be manipulated, or simply misbehave, and without global limits a single run can exhaust an API quota, run up a large bill, or invoke tools you never meant to expose. The policy layer bounds all of these at once and gives operators an instant stop, which is often a prerequisite for running agents against paid APIs and shared infrastructure.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of the dispatcher as a doorman with a clipboard and a meter. The clipboard is the allow list — your name isn't on it, you don't get in. The meter tracks how often you've entered and how much you've spent, and cuts you off at the limit. And there's a big red button behind the desk that locks every door at once. Nothing gets past the doorman without being checked against all of it.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Enforcing that an agent may only call an allowlisted set of tools, capping a session at N tool calls per minute, giving each user a daily token/dollar budget the agent can't exceed, and wiring a kill switch to a dashboard toggle so on-call can halt all agent activity during an incident.
foundations.performanceImpact: Policy checks are in-memory counter lookups and set membership tests — negligible next to a tool's I/O or an LLM call. At scale the counters move to a shared store (e.g. Redis) for accuracy across processes, adding a small network round-trip per call that is still tiny compared with the work being gated.
commonUseCases: Allowlisting the exact set of tools an agent may invoke
Per-user/session rate limits to protect downstream APIs
Per-user/session token and dollar budgets to cap cost
A kill switch to halt all agent activity during an incident

commonMisconceptions.myth: A deny list of dangerous tools is enough.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Deny lists always miss a case — a new, renamed, or hallucinated tool slips through. Default-deny with an explicit allow list fails closed, so anything unlisted is automatically refused.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Rate limits and budgets can be checked inside each tool.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Per-tool checks drift and get forgotten, and can't enforce a shared per-user/session ceiling. A single dispatcher with shared counters is the only place these limits hold consistently.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A kill switch is overkill if the other limits exist.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Limits bound steady-state behavior, but incidents need an instant, global stop that doesn't wait for budgets to drain. The kill switch is a distinct, first-class control for exactly those moments.

solution.code:
from collections import defaultdict

class Dispatcher:
    def __init__(self, allow, max_calls, max_spend):
        self.allow = set(allow)
        self.max_calls = max_calls
        self.max_spend = max_spend
        self.killed = False
        self.counts = defaultdict(int)
        self.spend = defaultdict(float)

    def dispatch(self, user, action, cost, tool_fn, **kwargs):
        if self.killed:                                   # emergency stop first
            raise PermissionError("killed")
        if action not in self.allow:                      # default-deny allow list
            raise PermissionError("denied")
        if self.counts[user] + 1 > self.max_calls:        # per-user rate limit
            raise PermissionError("rate")
        if self.spend[user] + cost > self.max_spend:      # per-user budget
            raise PermissionError("budget")
        self.counts[user] += 1                            # meter usage...
        self.spend[user] += cost
        return tool_fn(**kwargs)                           # ...then run

codeLab.testHarness:
d = Dispatcher(allow={"search"}, max_calls=2, max_spend=1.0)

# allowed call runs and meters usage
assert d.dispatch("u1", "search", 0.4, lambda: "ok") == "ok"
assert d.counts["u1"] == 1 and abs(d.spend["u1"] - 0.4) < 1e-9

# denied: action not on allow list
try:
    d.dispatch("u1", "delete", 0.0, lambda: "x"); raise AssertionError
except PermissionError as e:
    assert str(e) == "denied"

# denied: budget would be exceeded (0.4 + 0.8 > 1.0)
try:
    d.dispatch("u1", "search", 0.8, lambda: "x"); raise AssertionError
except PermissionError as e:
    assert str(e) == "budget"

# denied: kill switch
d.killed = True
try:
    d.dispatch("u1", "search", 0.1, lambda: "x"); raise AssertionError
except PermissionError as e:
    assert str(e) == "killed"
print("all tests passed")

theory.question: What belongs in an agent's policy layer, and why enforce it in one dispatcher rather than inside each tool?
theory.directAnswer: The policy layer holds a default-deny allow/deny list of tools, per-user/session rate limits, per-user/session token/dollar budgets, and a global kill switch. You enforce it in a single dispatcher because per-tool checks drift, get forgotten, and can't hold a shared per-caller ceiling — one chokepoint gives consistent, auditable, unbypassable enforcement with usage metered in one place.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A mediation component that authorizes every tool call against tool-allow rules, rate limits, and budgets, plus an emergency stop.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: An autonomous agent can loop, be manipulated, or misbehave, and without global controls a single run can exhaust an API quota, run up a bill, or invoke tools you never meant to expose.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The dispatcher intercepts each call and checks, in order, the kill switch, the allow/deny list (default-deny), the caller's rate limit over a window, and the caller's remaining budget; only if all pass does it run the tool and record the call and cost against shared counters.

theory.whyImportant: It bounds cost, throughput, and capability at once and gives operators an instant stop, which is often a prerequisite for running agents against paid APIs and shared infrastructure.
theory.realWorldExample: A production agent may call only six allowlisted tools, is capped at 30 tool calls/minute per session and $5/day per user, and a dashboard toggle flips a kill switch that halts all agent activity during an incident.

followUps.question: Where do the counters live at scale?
followUps.answer: In a shared store like Redis so rate and budget limits are accurate across multiple processes and instances, not just within one worker's memory.

followUps.question: Why keep the kill switch separate from budgets?
followUps.answer: Budgets bound steady-state spend, but incidents need an immediate global stop that doesn't wait for a budget to drain; the kill switch is a distinct first-class control.

theory.question: How do you design rate and spend limits so one runaway agent can't starve others or produce an unbounded bill?
theory.directAnswer: Scope the counters to the right key (user and session, sometimes per tool), check the limit before executing and meter usage only on success, and estimate each call's cost against a remaining budget so a call that would exceed is refused. Keep counters in a shared store and check budget before rate before running so a stuck loop is stopped early and cheaply.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A metering design that bounds both throughput (calls per window) and cost (tokens/dollars) per caller scope.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: A looping or manipulated agent can call a tool thousands of times or drive large model spend; per-caller limits contain the damage to that caller instead of the whole system.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: For rate, keep timestamps (or a counter with a window) per key and reject once the count in the window hits the limit; for budget, hold spent and limit per key, deny when spent + estimated_cost > limit, and commit spend only after the call is authorized to run.

theory.whyImportant: It converts unbounded failure modes (quota exhaustion, surprise bills, downstream overload) into predictable, per-caller ceilings the agent physically cannot cross.
theory.realWorldExample: A single misconfigured agent entered a tool-call loop; the per-session rate limit cut it off after 30 calls/minute and its $5 budget capped the incident's cost, while other users were unaffected.

followUps.question: Why check the limit before running the tool?
followUps.answer: So a call that would exceed the budget or rate is refused before incurring cost or side effects, rather than discovering the breach after the money's spent.

followUps.question: How do you handle cost you can only know after the call?
followUps.answer: Reserve an estimated cost up front, then reconcile with the actual usage after the call, refunding or charging the difference against the budget.

scenario.question: Overnight, one customer's agent entered a loop calling your paid search API tens of thousands of times, blowing the monthly quota and generating a large bill before anyone noticed. How would you build a policy layer so this can't recur?
scenario.directAnswer: Put every tool call through a policy-enforcing dispatcher with a default-deny allow list, per-user and per-session rate limits (calls per minute) and token/dollar budgets checked before execution, shared counters in Redis for cross-process accuracy, a kill switch wired to on-call, and alerting when a caller approaches its limits so a loop is stopped and surfaced within minutes rather than overnight.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A global governance layer that bounds throughput and spend per caller and gives operators an instant stop and early warning.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: The agent had an unbounded ability to call a paid tool, so a single loop translated directly into quota exhaustion and cost with no ceiling or alarm.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The dispatcher checks kill switch, allow list, rate limit, and budget before each call; counters live in a shared store so limits hold across workers; crossing a budget/rate threshold denies further calls and emits an alert; the kill switch lets on-call halt everything immediately.

scenario.whyImportant: It shows layering fast automatic ceilings (rate/budget) with a manual global stop (kill switch) and observability, so both the machine and the operator can contain a runaway.
scenario.realWorldExample: After deploying the dispatcher, a later loop hit the per-session rate limit within a minute, its budget capped the spend at a few dollars, an alert paged on-call, and the kill switch was available but never needed.

followUps.question: Why did in-memory counters fail here originally?
followUps.answer: With multiple worker processes, per-process counters each allow the full limit, so the effective limit multiplies; shared counters in Redis give one accurate ceiling across all workers.

followUps.question: What alert fires before the hard limit?
followUps.answer: A threshold alert (e.g. at 80% of budget or rate) so operators can investigate a runaway before it's fully cut off, catching misbehavior earlier than the hard denial.

coding.question: Write a sliding-window rate limiter that allows at most `limit` calls per `window` seconds per key, returning True if the call is permitted (and recording it) or False if it would exceed the limit.
coding.thoughtProcess: A sliding window is more accurate than a fixed bucket, so I keep a list of timestamps per key. On each call I drop timestamps older than the window, compare the remaining count to the limit, and only append the new timestamp (recording the call) when it's under the limit. Recording only on success means a denied call doesn't consume a slot, and per-key storage isolates one caller's usage from another's.

solution.code:
import time
from collections import defaultdict

class RateLimiter:
    def __init__(self, limit: int, window: float = 60.0):
        self.limit = limit
        self.window = window
        self._hits = defaultdict(list)   # key -> [timestamps]

    def allow(self, key: str, now: float | None = None) -> bool:
        now = time.time() if now is None else now
        hits = self._hits[key]
        # drop timestamps outside the sliding window
        self._hits[key] = [t for t in hits if now - t < self.window]
        if len(self._hits[key]) >= self.limit:
            return False                 # would exceed -> deny, don't record
        self._hits[key].append(now)      # record only on success
        return True

if __name__ == "__main__":
    rl = RateLimiter(limit=2, window=10.0)
    print(rl.allow("u1", now=0))    # True
    print(rl.allow("u1", now=1))    # True
    print(rl.allow("u1", now=2))    # False -- 2 in window already
    print(rl.allow("u1", now=12))   # True -- first two aged out

lineByLine: The limiter stores a list of hit timestamps per key so each caller is metered independently.
allow accepts an optional now so the logic is deterministically testable without real sleeps.
It filters out timestamps older than the window, implementing the sliding window rather than a coarse fixed bucket.
If the surviving count already meets the limit, it returns False and does not record the call, so a denied call consumes no slot.
Otherwise it appends the current timestamp (recording the call) and returns True.
The __main__ block shows two calls passing, the third denied, and a later call succeeding once the earliest hits age out.
coding.timeComplexity: O(k) per call where k is the hits currently in the window for that key (the filter step).
coding.spaceComplexity: O(k) per key for the retained timestamps; total O(sum of active windows across keys).

followUps.question: How would you make this correct across multiple processes?
followUps.answer: Move the per-key window to a shared store like Redis (e.g. a sorted set of timestamps with ZREMRANGEBYSCORE), so all workers share one accurate count instead of each holding its own.

followUps.question: How would you bound memory for many idle keys?
followUps.answer: Evict keys whose lists become empty after filtering, or use a TTL on the shared-store entries so stale keys expire automatically.

keyTakeaways: A policy layer governs the whole agent — allow/deny of tools, rate limits, and budgets — above and beyond per-tool sandboxing.
Use a default-deny allow list so unknown, renamed, or hallucinated tools fail closed rather than slipping through.
Meter rate and token/dollar spend per user and per session, checking the limit before execution so a runaway loop is cut off early.
Provide a kill switch as a distinct, instant global stop for incidents — don't rely on budgets draining.
Enforce everything in one policy dispatcher the agent can't bypass, with shared counters at scale and alerts before hard limits trip.
